entry.evidence: So far it remains unclear whether these differences are due to variations in warming rates in individual models or whether local feedback mechanisms

sequences.source_document: g22_W4284885982.xml.txt (published text), with figures from the published PDF

steps.action: The authors pose the question of why projections under similar greenhouse-gas scenarios give large differences in 21st-century ice-shelf surface melt.
steps.quote: So far it remains unclear whether these differences are due to variations in warming rates in individual models

steps.action: They state two rival explanations: differences in ESM warming rates, or local feedback mechanisms of the [...] .
steps.quote: [...] energy budget could also play a notable role

steps.action: They take the phenomenon, a melt spread at the same warming rate, from their own earlier MAR projections (Kittel et al. 2021; Gilbert and Kittel 2021).
steps.quote: projected melt changes can vary considerably even at the same rate of warming

steps.action: They use the regional climate model MARv3.11. Its Antarctic set-up and its evaluation against weather stations, satellite melt and cloud cover come from their earlier papers.
steps.quote: In this study, we used MARv3.11

steps.action: They compare MAR cloud water paths with the CloudSat–CALIPSO product (Figs. S1, S2) and find too little liquid and too much ice water path. They argue the bias is common to all downscalings and largely cancels in comparisons between them.
steps.quote: this bias affects all simulations in an equivalent way

steps.action: They design the experiment. The SEB is simplified to SWN+LWN+LHF+SHF, neglecting diffusion and refreezing (§2.1.1 ¶3). MAR is forced by two CMIP5 and two CMIP6 ESMs under RCP8.5/SSP5-8.5 at 35 km over 1975–2100, with DJF anomalies taken against 1981–2010.
steps.quote: We selected models from both CMIP5 and CMIP6 using the highest emission scenario

steps.action: They run the four MAR projections and obtain cumulative ice-shelf melt increases that differ by a factor of about 3.9.
steps.quote: We find a factor of ∼ 3.9 between the lowest and highest cumulative melt changes over the 21st century

steps.action: They break the melt and SEB changes down by sector (AP, EAIS, WAIS; Figure 1, p. 2659). The WAIS dominates the spread, and there net longwave explains the differences.
steps.quote: only LWN is projected to strongly increase and explains uncertainties in melt

steps.action: They compare melt with ECS and with each ESM's Antarctic warming (Figure 2, p. 2660). CNRM-CM6-1 gives more melt than the others at the same warming rate.
steps.quote: MAR forced by CNRM-CM6-1 still simulates a larger melt increase for the same warming rate than the other experiments

steps.action: They reject warming rate as the sole explanation of the spread. Warming is kept as the main control on absolute differences.
steps.quote: other local physical mechanisms have to be involved in addition to ESM warming rates

steps.action: They narrow the question to the drivers of downwelling longwave differences over the WAIS. The analysis focuses on the CNRM-CM6-1 and CESM2 pair, which have similar ECS and similar Antarctic warming.
steps.quote: We therefore analyse the factors behind LWN and more precisely behind LWD differences over the WAIS

steps.action: They list the candidate drivers of the LWD increase: atmospheric temperature, greenhouse gases including water vapour, and cloud optical thickness. Anthropogenic greenhouse forcing is set aside because both scenarios give the same radiative forcing.
steps.quote: mainly due to higher atmospheric temperature, larger greenhouse gas concentrations including water vapour, and optically thicker clouds

steps.action: They treat the atmosphere as a longwave-opaque black body to bound the largest LWD difference that atmospheric temperature alone could produce (Sect. S4, Table S1).
steps.quote: Approximating the atmosphere as a longwave-opaque and black body (see Sect. S4), we estimated the maximal potential contribution of the atmospheric temperature

steps.action: They reject atmospheric temperature and water vapour as drivers of the spread at a given warming rate. Temperature explains at most 31% of the CESM2/CNRM-CM6-1 LWD difference, and water vapour rises alike in all runs, following Clausius–Clapeyron (Figure 3, p. 2661).
steps.quote: could not explain more than 31 % of modelled future LWD differences

steps.action: They examine cloud cover and cloud optical depth changes over the WAIS (Figure 4, p. 2662; Figure 3c). CNRM-CM6-1 has the largest increases in both, and its COD rises more at equal warming.
steps.quote: MAR driven by CNRM-CM6-1 simulates stronger changes in COD than other experiments for equivalent near-surface warming rates

steps.action: They fit exponential LWD–COD relations for each experiment (R² ≥ 0.98; Figure 5, p. 2663) and infer that LWD saturates only at COD values not reached before 2100.
steps.quote: the sensitivity of the LWD increase would progressively stop for (very) large increases in COD

steps.action: They examine ice and liquid water path changes against ESM warming (Figures 6 and 7, p. 2663). The largest LWP increase is in CNRM-CM6-1 and the largest IWP increase in CESM2.
steps.quote: MAR driven by CNRM-CM6-1 projects a stronger increase in LWP

steps.action: They contrast CESM2 (more ice) with CNRM-CM6-1 (more liquid) and attribute the LWD spread at equal warming to liquid water path, through the dependence of cloud emissivity on liquid content.
steps.quote: The different increases in LWP control the spread in projected LWD for the same warming rate.

steps.action: They check that column-mean humidity and temperature changes are similar in the CESM2 and CNRM-CM6-1 runs over the WAIS (Table S2). This removes warming as a confound for the phase comparison.
steps.quote: This enables a direct comparison, removing the influence of global warming on potential differences.

steps.action: They examine humidity profiles at the lateral boundaries and the vertical profiles of snow and droplet content (Figure 8, p. 2664; Figs. S5, S6). CESM2 has more humidity above 2000 m and CNRM-CM6-1 has more low-level humidity advection.
steps.quote: the future CNRM-CM6-1 atmosphere is characterised by stronger low-level humidity advection

steps.action: They refine the claim into a causal chain: warmer low-level humidity advection forms liquid droplets, which raise LWP, COD and LWD, and so melt.
steps.quote: The preferential future increase in low-level water droplets in the CNRM-CM6-1 experiment finally induces a stronger surface melt

steps.action: They show that SWN increases despite lower SWD because albedo falls. CNRM-CM6-1 has a stronger albedo decrease over the WAIS at a given warming (Figure 9, p. 2665), which they link to the snowmelt–albedo feedback.
steps.quote: MAR forced by CNRM-CM6-1 projects a stronger albedo decrease over the WAIS sector

steps.action: They rerun MAR forced by CNRM-CM6-1 with rainfall set to zero and find no difference in the albedo and melt result.
steps.quote: a sensitivity experiment in MAR forced by CNRM-CM6-1 where rainfall amounts were set to 0 reveals no difference

steps.action: They reject differences in liquid precipitation as an extra amplifier of the melt differences, within the projected precipitation rates.
steps.quote: differences in liquid precipitation due to clouds do not further strengthen melt differences

steps.action: They propose, by analogy with the Greenland ablation zone, that a darker surface in warmer climates could reverse the summer cloud radiative effect. This is not tested.
steps.quote: These warmer conditions could reverse the summer cloud radiative effect, reducing melt

steps.action: They keep the claim: clouds, through liquid water content and phase, drive the melt spread for a given warming, via LWD and the melt–albedo feedback.
steps.quote: we highlight the importance of cloud water content and phase to explain the differences in projected melt for a given warming

steps.action: They limit the claim: no projection is more plausible than another, the result holds for clouds as simulated in MAR, and drifting snow and the LWP bias are possible further influences.
steps.quote: none of these projections is more plausible than any other

tree.answer: Large spread in projected ice-shelf melt under equivalent high-emission forcing, including at the same warming rate
No; the spread exists only in model projections (MAR downscalings of ESMs)
Explain the physical (SEB) drivers of the melt spread
Yes: ESM warming rate versus local SEB/cloud feedbacks; then temperature, water vapour, greenhouse gases and cloud properties as LWD drivers; liquid precipitation as an albedo amplifier
Partly: warming alone predicts one melt-versus-warming curve, and a black-body bound caps the temperature contribution at 31%
Conditions set in the model by choice of ESM forcing and one rainfall-off sensitivity run
Partly: rainfall-zero ablation and matched-warming control; MAR physics itself not varied, one RCM only
Cloud liquid water/phase kept as best explanation of the melt spread at a given warming, within MAR
Not documented; no review file or open discussion supplied

end.claim: Within MAR, differences in future ice-shelf melt at the same warming rate are driven by cloud properties, especially larger liquid water content from low-level humidity advection. This raises LWD and melt, which the snowmelt–albedo feedback amplifies.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing melt against ESM warming across the four downscalings (Fig. 2) showed CNRM-CM6-1 melting more at the same warming rate. Without this, warming rate alone would explain the spread and no cloud-driver claim would arise.

gates.evidence: The four-ESM design comes from earlier work selecting for warming diversity (§2.1.2 ¶2), not from the cloud hypothesis. Only the rainfall-zero run (§3.3 ¶2) was directed by a stated hypothesis. The warming-only and temperature rivals could have explained the spread (Fig. 2; black-body bound, §3.2.1 ¶1), so the attribution faced diagnostics it could have failed. The cloud claim itself is not tested against independent data or other models, and nothing was fixed before the runs.

imports.item: Black-body, longwave-opaque approximation of the atmosphere to bound the temperature contribution to LWD
Clausius–Clapeyron relation for water vapour increase with warming
Exponential regression of LWD on COD with determination coefficients

novelty_claims.quote: A first comparison with the CloudSat–CALIPSO product

limits: No review file or open discussion was supplied. The Acknowledgements and Review statement mention three referees, so changes made in review cannot be coded and Q9 is unanswered. All evidence is model output from one regional model (MAR) forced by four ESMs. MAR physics, including cloud microphysics, is never varied, and no second regional model is used. The claim is therefore conditional on clouds 'as simulated in MAR' (§4 ¶3). MAR underestimates present LWP and overestimates IWP against CloudSat–CALIPSO (§2.1 ¶2; §4 ¶3). The authors' argument that this bias cancels between downscalings is asserted, not tested (inference). Drifting snow is not modelled. The core attribution rests largely on one pair of runs (CNRM-CM6-1 versus CESM2). Supplementary material (Sect. S4, Tables S1–S2, Figs. S1–S6) was not supplied, so the black-body bound and the matched-humidity control are coded from the main text only. Sub-claims at other statuses: the LWD–COD exponential relation is regularity_in_range, valid within the simulated COD range up to 2100 (Fig. 5). That liquid precipitation does not amplify melt differences rests on one sensitivity run and holds only for the projected rain rates. The low-level humidity advection mechanism is best_explanation. The possible future reversal of the cloud radiative effect is an untested hypothesis. Composition is none_fits because conditions are set in a model, not found. Rivals are excluded one after another by diagnostics on a small forcing ensemble rather than by a single crucial test, so neither strong_inference nor trace_series fits.

disagreements.target: Temperature-based diagnostic of melt (Trusel et al., 2015)
disagreements.support: Their own and earlier MAR projections give different melt at the same warming rate, so warming alone is not a sufficient predictor (Fig. 2).
disagreements.quote: projected melt changes can vary considerably even at the same rate of warming

disagreements.target: Common practice of assessing the Antarctic sea-level contribution for specific warming rates (e.g. Pattyn et al., 2018)
disagreements.support: CNRM-CM6-1 and CESM2 have similar warming but different melt and hydrofracture-prone area, which the authors attribute to liquid-containing clouds.
disagreements.quote: liquid-containing clouds could lead to large uncertainties even for the same warming rate

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Including snow thermal diffusion and liquid water refreezing energy
alternatives_considered.reason: Focus on atmospheric factors; diffusion an order of magnitude smaller and does not contribute to surface melt; refreezing warms mainly deeper layers and its potential declines with runoff

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Radiative effect of rain; full snow concentration
alternatives_considered.reason: Rain droplets reach the surface within one radiative time step; snow-to-ice ratio set by effective radii
